title: Piper PA-44-180 Seminole — Emergency Procedures
description: Emergency procedures for the Piper PA-44-180 Seminole twin-engine trainer. Covers engine failure, engine fire, electrical emergencies, oil pressure loss, gear malfunctions, and single-engine operations. Memory items are marked and must be completed before consulting this checklist. The Seminole has counter-rotating propellers with no critical engine; single-engine performance is identical regardless of which engine fails. Each engine is fed by its own independent fuel system; the Seminole does not have crossfeed capability in standard configuration — consult the specific aircraft POH. All airspeeds (including Vyse/blue line and Vsse) must come from the POH. This document does not substitute for multi-engine training with a qualified instructor.

source.notes: No manufacturer document consulted. Written from general familiarity with the type.

known_issues.description: Contains no airspeeds, power settings, fuel quantities, or other numerical limitations — all must come from the specific aircraft POH. Vyse (blue line) is the single most critical speed in engine-out operations and must be known before flight.
Equipment variations exist across PA-44-180 airframes. Verify items against the specific aircraft before use. Some aircraft may have crossfeed capability not reflected here.

rights.notes: Manufacturer POH remains under copyright. This file does not reproduce its wording or selection of items.

sections.title: Engine Failure on Takeoff — Before or at Rotation
sections.condition: Engine failure during the takeoff roll or at the moment of rotation

items.text: An engine failure before reaching Vmc or Vyse with gear in transit is almost certainly not survivable as a continued takeoff. Abort unless airborne with positive control and altitude.
Throttles — both engines, close immediately
Brakes — apply firmly and progressively to stop on remaining runway
Mixture controls — both engines, idle cutoff
Fuel selectors — both engines, off
Ignition switches — both engines, off
Master switch
Evacuate aircraft if fire or other hazard present

sections.title: Engine Failure — After Liftoff (Airborne)
sections.condition: Engine failure after becoming airborne; aircraft below safe single-engine maneuvering altitude

items.text: Below Vyse and below a safe altitude, attempting to maintain flight on one engine may be impossible. A straight-ahead landing on available terrain may be the only survivable option. Do not attempt to turn back to the field below a safe altitude.
Airspeed — establish and maintain Vyse (blue line) or best available
Operating engine — advance throttle to full power
Dead engine — identify by direction of yaw and failed gauges (dead foot — dead engine)
Dead engine propeller — feather by advancing prop control to full forward then pulling to feather
Landing gear — retract to reduce drag
Flaps — retract if extended
Bank — 5 degrees toward the operating engine; maintain with rudder
Continue with Engine Failure in Flight checklist to secure failed engine
items.response: PROCEED TO ENGINE FAILURE IN FLIGHT

sections.title: Engine Failure in Flight — Identify / Verify / Feather / Secure
sections.condition: One engine loses power or stops during cruise or other in-flight phases

items.text: The four-step memory sequence is: IDENTIFY — VERIFY — FEATHER — SECURE. Complete all four steps before consulting the written checklist.
IDENTIFY — dead foot, dead engine: the foot with less or no rudder pressure is on the same side as the failed engine
VERIFY — advance throttle on the identified dead engine; confirm no power response and gauges confirm failure
FEATHER — move propeller control of the failed engine to feather
Airspeed — establish and maintain Vyse (blue line) or best climb/glide speed per POH
Bank — 5 degrees toward the operating engine to minimize rudder workload
Operating engine — confirm full power set
SECURE the failed engine:
SECURE — throttle on failed engine
SECURE — mixture on failed engine
SECURE — fuel selector on failed engine
SECURE — magnetos on failed engine
Alternator on failed engine
Cowl flap on failed engine — as required per POH
Declare emergency if appropriate — advise ATC of single-engine condition
Divert — plan landing at nearest suitable airport; do not delay

sections.title: Engine Fire in Flight
sections.condition: Fire warning light, flames, smoke, or unusual odor indicating an engine fire while airborne

items.text: Throttle — affected engine, close immediately
Fuel selector — affected engine, OFF
Mixture — affected engine, IDLE CUTOFF
Propeller — affected engine, FEATHER
Magnetos — affected engine, OFF
Alternator — affected engine, OFF
Airspeed — increase if possible to help extinguish fire by airflow; do not exceed Vne
Fire extinguisher — use if fire enters cabin
If fire extinguished — execute single-engine approach; do not restart the engine
If fire not extinguished — execute emergency descent; prepare for forced landing
Declare emergency — ATC notified

sections.title: Engine Fire on Ground
sections.condition: Fire in engine compartment during start or while taxiing

items.text: Throttle — affected engine, open briefly to draw fire back into intake, then close
Mixture — affected engine, IDLE CUTOFF
Fuel selector — affected engine, OFF
Ignition — affected engine, OFF
Master switch
Evacuate aircraft immediately; move upwind
Fire extinguisher — use if trained; do not approach a fully involved engine fire
Emergency services — notify airport fire department

sections.title: Electrical Fire / Smoke in Cockpit
sections.condition: Burning smell, smoke, or visible arcing from electrical equipment

items.text: Master switch
Avionics master
All electrical switches and circuit breakers
Vents — open to clear smoke from cockpit; consider passenger oxygen if smoke is heavy
Fire extinguisher — discharge if fire is visible
If smoke clears — systematically restore essential electrical items one at a time to isolate the faulty circuit
Land at nearest suitable airport
Declare emergency and notify ATC

sections.title: Loss of Oil Pressure — One Engine
sections.condition: Oil pressure gauge on one engine reads in the yellow or red arc, or oil pressure warning light illuminates

items.text: Low oil pressure may precede engine failure by a short time. Begin planning for single-engine operations immediately. Do not wait for the engine to fail.
Identify affected engine — note which oil pressure gauge is reading low
Oil temperature — check; rising temperature confirms oil loss or internal failure
Power on affected engine — reduce to minimum required to maintain flight; do not shut down prematurely unless failure is imminent
Airspeed — prepare to establish Vyse if engine fails
Nearest suitable airport — identify and divert; do not continue to planned destination
If engine seizes or fails — execute engine failure in flight procedures
Declare emergency and notify ATC
items.response: MAYDAY OR PAN-PAN DECLARED; ATC NOTIFIED

sections.title: Carburetor Ice — One or Both Engines
sections.condition: Unexplained loss of RPM or rough running, especially in humid conditions or when reducing power

items.text: The O-360 is a carbureted engine. Carburetor ice can form at temperatures well above freezing in humid conditions. Partial ice may cause rough running before total power loss.
Affected engine — apply full carburetor heat immediately; do not cycle on and off
Carburetor heat — expect a momentary further RPM drop as ice melts, followed by smooth power restoration
If power does not restore — maintain carb heat and prepare for engine failure procedures
Altitude and terrain — assess options for forced landing if both engines affected
After power restored — maintain carburetor heat until clear of icing conditions per POH
Monitor both engines for recurrence of roughness

sections.title: Forced Landing — Power-Off
sections.condition: Both engines have failed or remaining power is insufficient to reach an airport

items.text: A dual-engine failure is extremely rare. Confirm both engines are truly failed before accepting a forced landing. Check fuel selectors, mixture, and magnetos.
Best glide speed — establish immediately per POH
Landing area — select best available field or road; favor into-wind and uphill if possible
Fuel selectors — confirm both on correct tanks; attempt restart if cause is fuel starvation
Mixture — RICH for restart attempt
Ignition — BOTH; attempt restart if time and altitude permit
Mayday — declare on 121.5 MHz; advise position, altitude, intentions
Transponder — 7700
Fuel selectors — OFF before landing to reduce fire risk
Mixture — IDLE CUTOFF
Ignition switches — OFF just before touchdown
Master switch — OFF just before touchdown
Doors — unlatch before touchdown to prevent jamming
Seat belts and shoulder harnesses — confirm tight

sections.title: Gear Unsafe / Abnormal Gear Indication
sections.condition: One or more gear position lights fail to show green after gear extension, or red unsafe light illuminates

items.text: Airspeed — reduce to below gear operating speed per POH
Gear handle — cycle UP then DOWN; allow adequate time for system to respond
Circuit breakers — check gear-related breakers; reset if popped
Gear position lights — check bulbs by pressing the test button if equipped
If no green after normal extension — refer to emergency gear extension procedure
Declare emergency and notify ATC; request emergency equipment standby

sections.title: Emergency Gear Extension
sections.condition: Normal gear extension fails; gear not locked down; use manual/emergency extension system

items.text: Airspeed — reduce to minimum safe airspeed per POH; below emergency extension speed
Gear handle — ensure in DOWN position
Emergency gear extension — locate and activate the manual extension pump or override per POH specific to this aircraft
Pump or pull override — operate per POH until three green lights illuminate
items.response: THREE GREEN CONFIRMED OR BEST INDICATION OBTAINED

items.text: If gear still not confirmed down and locked — prepare for gear-up landing; follow forced-landing precautions
Notify ATC of gear status; request foam or emergency equipment as applicable

sections.title: Single-Engine Approach and Landing
sections.condition: One engine inoperative; planning and executing approach and landing

items.text: A go-around on one engine at low altitude and slow airspeed is extremely hazardous. Commit to landing once established on final. Plan ahead so go-around is not required.
Operating engine — confirm full power available; do not reduce power on approach prematurely
Airspeed — maintain at or above Vyse until landing assured; use POH single-engine approach speed on final
items.response: AT OR ABOVE POH APPROACH SPEED

items.text: Flaps — extend incrementally; be cautious with full flaps due to increased drag on one engine
Gear — extend with adequate altitude and airspeed to assure landing; expect higher drag
Runway — aim for a long runway if available; do not aim for the threshold; aim slightly beyond
items.response: LONG RUNWAY SELECTED; ADJUSTED AIM POINT

items.text: Final approach — keep it flat and stable; avoid a steep descent that requires large power changes
GUMPS check — Gas, Undercarriage, Mixture, Props, Seat belts/Switches
Operating engine throttle — reduce to idle only over the runway threshold when landing is assured
Touchdown — land positively; do not float; use available braking

sections.title: Engine-Out Go-Around
sections.condition: Go-around required with one engine inoperative — extremely hazardous; avoid if possible

items.text: A single-engine go-around from a low, slow final is one of the most demanding maneuvers in multi-engine flying. Do not initiate unless a safe landing is truly impossible and altitude permits. The risk of losing control is very high near the ground at low speed.
Operating engine — full power immediately and smoothly
Pitch attitude — establish climb attitude per POH; avoid extreme pitch
Airspeed — accelerate to Vyse immediately; never allow speed to fall below Vmc
Flaps — retract incrementally per POH as airspeed builds
Gear — retract after positive rate of climb is confirmed
Directional control — maintain bank 5 degrees into operating engine; use rudder trim if available
ATC — notify of go-around and single-engine status
Plan next approach — configure for a wider, higher pattern to allow time and altitude
